topic: Build your own: dependency injection framework

questions.question: At its core, what lookup structure does a DI container need to resolve a dependency?
options: A list of every created instance, searched in the order they were created
A map from key (type plus qualifier) to a provider for that dependency
A map from each class name to the single shared instance of that class
A tree of Activities, each holding the constructors for its own screen objects
questions.explanation: Resolution means looking up a binding by key and asking its provider for an instance; the provider decides whether to create a new one or return a cached one. Keying by class alone breaks as soon as you need two Strings or two OkHttpClients with qualifiers. Storing instances directly would rule out factory bindings.

questions.question: `OkHttpClient` is registered as a factory binding, so each injection creates a new one. What is the practical problem?
options: OkHttpClient cannot be constructed off the main thread, so injection blocks it
Factory bindings make constructor injection of the client impossible to use
Each client has its own connection and thread pools, so nothing is reused
The graph fails validation, because factory bindings may not have dependencies
questions.explanation: OkHttpClient is designed to be shared: its connection pool and dispatcher are only useful when reused. A singleton (or app-scoped) binding fixes it, and derived clients can be built with `newBuilder()` to share the pool. Factories are fine for cheap, stateless or per-use objects.

questions.question: A singleton `AnalyticsRepository` depends on an Activity-scoped `ScreenTracker`. What should a well-designed DI framework do?
options: Reject the graph: a longer-lived scope must not depend on a shorter-lived one
Allow it, and recreate the singleton whenever the Activity itself is recreated
Allow it, and keep the first ScreenTracker alive for the rest of the app's lifetime
Silently create a fresh ScreenTracker for every call made on the singleton
questions.explanation: A singleton holding an Activity-scoped object either leaks that Activity or keeps using a stale one after rotation. Compile-time frameworks like Dagger reject this scope mismatch at build time. The fix is to invert it: pass the shorter-lived object as a method argument or inject a provider tied to the right scope.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of a compile-time codegen DI framework (like Dagger) over a runtime-resolved one?
options: Generated factories make the APK smaller than any runtime container could
Bindings can be swapped at runtime in production without rebuilding the app
It works without annotations, kapt/KSP or any other build configuration at all
Graph errors fail the build, and startup needs no reflection or graph building
questions.explanation: Codegen moves graph validation to compile time and emits plain factory code, so errors show up before shipping and startup does no reflective work. The costs are build time (kapt or KSP) and annotation boilerplate. Runtime containers are more flexible, and APK size depends on the app, not the approach.

questions.question: With Koin's plain runtime DSL (no compile-time verification plugin), a missing definition fails the Gradle build.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The plain DSL builds and resolves the graph at runtime, so a missing definition surfaces as an exception when that dependency is first requested. Teams typically add a test that checks the module configuration, or use Koin's annotation and compile-time checking options, to catch it earlier.

questions.question: `A` needs `B` in its constructor, and `B` needs `A`. How should a runtime DI framework detect this and how can the app break it?
options: Put a timeout on resolution, and break it by making both A and B singletons
Track keys being resolved and fail on a repeat; inject a Provider or Lazy for one side
It can't be detected; catch the StackOverflowError and retry the resolution
Compare the classes' hash codes, and break it with field injection on both sides of the pair
questions.explanation: Keeping a stack of in-progress keys finds a cycle the moment a key appears twice and gives a readable path like A -> B -> A. Injecting `Provider<A>` or `Lazy<A>` into B defers the lookup until after A exists, which breaks the construction cycle. Making both singletons does not help, because neither can finish construction first.

questions.question: Which are correct ways to make lazy singleton creation thread-safe in your container? Select all that apply.
options: A plain `if (instance == null) instance = create()` check, because DI only runs at startup
Caching instances in a WeakHashMap keyed by binding
A per-binding lock so creating unrelated singletons does not block each other
Double-checked locking with a `volatile` instance field
questions.explanation: Double-checked locking is correct only with `volatile`, which stops other threads from seeing a partly constructed instance, and per-binding locks avoid one slow constructor stalling everything. Unsynchronized checks can create two instances when background threads inject at the same time. Weak references let the GC drop a singleton, so a second instance appears later.

questions.question: A reflection-based container keys bindings by `Class`. Registering both `List<String>` and `List<Int>` causes a duplicate binding error. Why?
options: Kotlin does not allow two bindings of collection types within a single module
List bindings are always singletons and so they cannot be given qualifiers
Type arguments are erased, so both keys are just `List` at runtime
The container sorts keys alphabetically, and String sorts ahead of Int
questions.explanation: `List<String>::class` and `List<Int>::class` are the same runtime class. Frameworks keep the full type with a type token or `typeOf<T>()`, or use qualifiers. Code generators like Dagger see full types at compile time, so this does not happen there.

questions.question: Constructor injection makes a class's dependencies explicit and lets tests build it with fakes without starting the DI framework.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. With every dependency in the constructor, a test just calls the constructor with fakes. Field injection or service-locator lookups hide dependencies and usually need the container running in tests.

questions.question: Your DI framework supports Android-aware scopes. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A Fragment-scoped binding outlives its host Activity
A ViewModel-scoped binding survives configuration changes such as rotation
Application-scoped singletons are per process, so a second app process gets its own instances
An Activity-scoped binding is recreated when the Activity is recreated on rotation
questions.explanation: ViewModel scope is tied to the ViewModelStore, which survives configuration changes, while Activity scope follows the Activity instance. Singletons live in a process's memory, so a multi-process app has separate copies, a common surprise with background services. A Fragment cannot outlive the Activity that hosts it.
